title: Against the Clock
tagline: A pack of cards, a clock and a room full of silent competitors. How to get faster without getting sloppy.
card: What happens in a speed event, where the time goes, and how to train for pace without losing accuracy.
goal: you will find out where your time goes when you memorise, remove the slowest step, and train in short timed rounds that build speed safely.

left_off.q: What is the difference between recognising and recalling?
left_off.a: Recognising is a feeling of familiarity when you see it; recalling is bringing it out with nothing in front of you.

left_off.q: How long of a one-hour study session should be spent testing yourself?
Name the five steps of the study cycle.
left_off.a: Understand, picture, place, test yourself, come back.

text: A large hall. Rows of tables. At each table there is a competitor with a pack of cards face down in front of them, a stopwatch, and a pair of ear defenders. The room is silent. When the signal comes, every competitor turns over the pack and begins.

This is the speed cards event, one of the most watched at memory championships. The task: look at a shuffled pack of fifty-two cards and learn the order as fast as you can. When you are ready you stop the clock, hand over the pack, and later you must put a second, new pack into the same order. Both the time and the accuracy count.

check.q: What must a speed cards competitor do?
check.a: Learn the order of a shuffled pack as fast as possible, stop the clock, and later arrange a fresh pack in the same order.

parts.talk: Would you rather be fast and sometimes wrong, or slow and always right? In which situations?

text: In recent years the best competitors have got the time for a whole pack below thirteen seconds. That is about a quarter of a second for each card. It sounds impossible, and it would be, if each card needed a new idea. But it does not.

The answer is that nothing new happens at all. Every card is already a fixed picture, and every place is already a fixed place. The competitor is not inventing. They are looking up pictures and putting them in places they have walked a thousand times. The work was done in training, long before the day.

check.q: How can a competitor learn a pack in about a quarter of a second per card?
check.a: Nothing is invented on the day: each card is already a fixed picture and each place is a fixed place, so it is look-up and placing.

parts.talk: What skill have you practised so much that you now do it without thinking? How long did it take?

text: The most important lesson of speed is the least obvious. You do not get faster by trying to go faster. You get faster by finding the one step that is slow, and making it automatic, and then finding the next.
In this room you will do exactly that, using ordinary words and pictures instead of cards. You will time yourself, find where the seconds go, and train in short rounds that raise your speed in steps.

check.a: Find the slowest step, make it automatic, then find the next one.

parts.talk: What would you like to be able to do ten times faster?

words.m: the narrowest point, where things slow down. The bottleneck is the look-up.
to practise something again and again.
the quality of being correct. Speed without accuracy is useless.
to measure how long something takes.

source: The speed cards event is part of the standard World Memory Championship programme. Records change; 'below thirteen seconds' is the order of magnitude. Our own account.

items: Accuracy first. Do not time yourself until you can do the task correctly at a slow pace.
Short rounds. Thirty to sixty seconds, then stop and rest. Many short rounds beat one long one.
Raise the speed by about a tenth each time. If you make errors, go back.
Keep a log. Write the time and the number of mistakes. Progress is visible.

method.title: A timed round with words
method.given: Ten words in sixty seconds: tiger, anchor, violin, pepper, rocket, mirror, candle, bridge, lantern, saddle.
lines: Each is already a picture. No decision.
One action and one sense: a tiger roaring at a mirror.
Ten places on a route you know by heart.
At the end, walk the route once and say each word.
method.pic: Ten quick scenes, six seconds each, on a route that is already automatic.

method.x: Describe the four steps of memorising an item, and say which of them is slowest for you.

try.title: Find the bottleneck
try.prompt: Match each symptom to the step that is slow.
pairs: You hesitate over which picture a card is
You spend ages making each picture perfect
You get lost in your route
You keep going back to check earlier items

try.title: A timed round
try.prompt: Take the ten words from the example. Write one very short scene for each (a few words only). Try to finish in two minutes. Then write your time.
try.model: tiger roaring at mirror; anchor in coffee cup; violin sawn in half; pepper sneezing; rocket in a bath; mirror dancing; candle melting on a head; bridge walking; lantern singing; saddle on a giraffe.
checks: I wrote ten very short scenes.

try.title: Your training log
try.prompt: Design a one-line log for your practice. What will you write each day (date, task, time, mistakes)? Write an example entry.
try.model: Monday 18 Oct: 10 words, 52 seconds, 1 mistake (candle). Plan: raise to 10 words in 47 seconds.
checks: There is a date and a task.
There is a number of mistakes.

try.q: A learner is fast but makes many mistakes. What should they do?
opts: Slow down until the accuracy is back, then raise the speed again
try.why: Accuracy first, then speed in small steps.

try.title: Walk the route fast
try.prompt: Walk your palace route in your head as fast as you can, naming each place. Do it three times and see if it gets quicker.

quiz.q: What is the best length for a training round?
opts: About thirty to sixty seconds, then rest
quiz.why: Short rounds with rests build speed safely.

quiz.q: When should you start timing yourself?
